European.caption: European 4-in-1 the most basic European weave.
European.text: European weaves are inspired by weaves historically worn as armour originating in Europe. European weaves tend to have a noticeable grain due to the rings alternating direction in each row. Below is a list of articles about weaves of the European family.

Japanese.caption: Japanese 4-in-1 the most basic Japanese weave.
Japanese.text: Japanese weaves are inspired by weaves historically worn as armour in Japan. Japanese weaves are characterized by rings joining at 90-degree angles and tend to be geometric. Below is a list of articles about weaves of the Japanese family.

Persian.caption: Full Persian 6-in-1 a historic weave that serves as a foundation of the persian weave family.
Persian.text: Members of the Persian weave family can be distinguished by their use of stacked rings, usually having two sets of pairs, each moving in opposite directions.

Mage.caption: Magemaille is the foundation of all mage weaves.
Mage.text: Members of the Mage weave family are characterized by having slants alternate so they don't stack.

Mobius.caption: A Mobius Ball, the most basic of Mobius weaves.
Mobius.text: Members of the Mobius weave family use Mobius Balls with three or more rings where a single ring would work, adding some flair.

Rhino.caption: Rhinos Snorting Drano the origin of the Rhino family of weaves.
Rhino.text: Members of the Rhino weave family are characterized by their frequent use of around-the-eye connections.

Helm.caption: Helm Chain the origin of the Helm weave family.
Helm.text: Members of the Helm weave family can be distinguished by their use of small rings inside of larger rings and the larger rings orbiting around those small rings.

weave.caption: The Japanese 4-in-1 weave, a very basic weave.
weave.text: In chainmail, a weave is an infinitely repeating pattern and unique of rings, where each ring meaningfully contributes such that removing one ring drastically changes its characteristics.

eye.caption: The eyes formed by the red ring and yellow rings are highlighted purple.
eye.text: In chainmail, an eye is the area of overlap of the interiors of two or more rings. Typically, when adding rings in relation to an eye, you either add ring(s) around the eye, through the eye or both.

chain.text: In chainmail, a chain is a weave that is infinitely repeatable in one direction.

sheet.text: In chainmail, a sheet is a weave that is infinitely repeatable in two directions that are perpendicular to each other.

solid.text: In chainmail, a solid is a weave that is infinitely repeatable in three directions that are all perpendicular to each other.

unit.text: In chainmail, a unit is a weave that is not infinitely repeatable in any direction, leaving you with a single item of a fixed size.

aspect_ratio.text: The Aspect Ratio(AR) is how large a ring is (relative to its wire thickness), where a higher AR means a larger ring. The formula to calculate it is Inner Diameter divided by Wire Diameter.

inner_diameter.text: The Inner Diameter(ID) of a ring is the diameter of the circle formed by the inside edge of a ring.

family.text: Weave families are groups of weaves sharing a set of defining characteristics.

wire_diameter.text: The Wire Diameter(WD) of a ring is the distance from the inner edge of the ring to the closest point on the outer edge of the ring.

mandrel_diameter.text: The Mandrel Diameter(MD) of a ring is the diameter of the mandrel on which the ring was wound. This approximates the true Inner Diameter of the ring; however, due to springback, it is not the same.

springback.text: Springback is when the wire coiled around a mandrel expands after it is no longer under tension. This makes the rings slightly larger than the mandrel they were wound on.

mandrel.text: A rod that you wrap wire around to form coils to cut into rings. You can use a wooden dowel however, using a strong material is beneficial as it will keep a more consistent size.

standard_wire_gauge.text: Standard Wire Gauge(SWG) is a wire gauge system that assigns a number to a specified thickness (Wire Diameter) of wire with a thicker wire having a smaller gauge. You can read more about it here.

american_wire_gauge.text: American Wire Gauge(AWG) is a wire gauge system that assigns a number to a specified thickness (Wire Diameter) of wire with a thicker wire having a smaller gauge. You can read more about it here.
